report.source_text: Lymph node biopsy revealed diffuse infiltration of small to medium-sized lymphocytes with rare nuclear irregularities, which distorted the nodal architecture. Giant cells with irregularly lobulated nuclei, like Reed-Sternberg cells, were scattered among the background lymphocytes (Fig. 1). Some macrophages and angiogenesis were also observed. On immunohistochemical analysis, the giant cells were positive for CD30 and CD15, and negative for CD3, CD20, PAX5, and Epstein-Barr virus-encoded RNA1 in situ hybridization (EBER-ISH). The background lymphocytes were positive for CD3, CD4, CD5, and CD25 (partially). These findings were consistent with lymphocyte-rich classic Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL).

report.source_text: Doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine (ABVD) were first administered because the diagnosis was cHL. However, after one cycle of ABVD, the treatment regimen was changed to pirarubicin, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, and prednisolone (THP-COP) due to the diagnosis changing to Hodgkin-like ATLL. During the first cycle of THP-COP, the patient developed drug induced eruptions and grade 3 febrile neutropenia. Considering these side effects, he refused a second cycle of THP-COP and decided to receive low-dose oral chemotherapy (400 mg of sobuzoxane, 25 mg of etoposide, and 10 mg of prednisolone for 3 days every 2-3 weeks) in an outpatient setting.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 56-year-old man with long-standing HAM/TSP (HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis) diagnosed at age 42 presented with right inguinal lymphadenopathy (3.0 cm, elastic-hard, poor mobility) at age 56. Initial laboratory findings showed elevated IL-2 receptor (1000 U/L), anti-HTLV-1 antibody positivity (ELISA and western blotting), and normal LDH. Lymph node biopsy revealed Hodgkin-like features with Reed-Sternberg-like giant cells (CD30+, CD15+, CD3-, CD20-, PAX5-, EBER-ISH-) and background CD3+CD4+CD5+CD25+ lymphocytes consistent with lymphocyte-rich classic Hodgkin lymphoma morphology. Critically, Southern blot analysis detected di-clonal proviral HTLV-1 DNA in both lymph node and peripheral blood, confirming HTLV-1 integration and establishing the diagnosis of ATLL rather than classic Hodgkin lymphoma. Peripheral blood showed appearance of atypical lymphoid cells (maximum 160/µl) and temporary elevation of IL-2 receptor (maximum 2018 U/L). CT imaging demonstrated stable disease over approximately 2 years. Treatment initially consisted of ABVD (1 cycle), then switched to THP-COP after diagnosis change to Hodgkin-like ATLL. Due to drug-induced eruptions and grade 3 febrile neutropenia, the patient declined further THP-COP and received low-dose oral chemotherapy (sobuzoxane 400 mg, etoposide 25 mg, prednisolone 10 mg for 3 days every 2-3 weeks) in an outpatient setting with stable disease maintained over approximately 2 years.
